---
title: "Example: seasonal liver plasticity in a treefrog"
bibliography: ../references.bib
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r library}
library(lagprotest)
```

This article analyzes a real data set with `lagged_protest()` and
`lagged_protest_pairs()`. The question is whether seasonal changes in the
liver of the treefrog *Dendropsophus minutus* track climate within the same
month or with a delay, and whether hepatic modules lead one another.

## The data

`dminutus_liver` holds monthly means of four hepatic modules and of
climate, from April 2016 to March 2017
[@francobelussi2026data; see `?dminutus_liver` for the variables]. Each
element is a matrix with 12 rows (months) and one column per variable.
Climate combines temperature, rainfall and humidity from BR-DWGD
[@xavier2022brdwgd], a drought index from TerraClimate
[@abatzoglou2018terraclimate], UV-B irradiance from glUV
[@beckmann2014gluv] and photoperiod.

```{r data}
sapply(dminutus_liver, dim)
```

The series span exactly one annual cycle, so the phase and cyclic schemes,
which treat the series as periodic with period *n*, apply without
truncation (`period` is not needed). With 12 time points, the power to
detect a lag is limited, and strong autocorrelation would make the phase
scheme somewhat liberal (see
[Choosing a permutation scheme](permutation-schemes.html)); the cyclic
scheme is used below as a conservative check.

## Contemporaneous concordance

Concordance within the same month is the lag-0 PROTEST for every pair of
data sets. With a single lag, the global p-value equals the raw one, and
`lagged_protest_pairs()` adjusts it across the ten pairs (Benjamini–Hochberg
by default):

```{r lag0}
lag0 <- lagged_protest_pairs(dminutus_liver, lags = 0, bidirectional = FALSE,
                             nperm = 9999, seed = 1)
knitr::kable(lag0[, c("x", "y", "m2", "r", "p.value", "p.global.adjusted")],
             digits = 3)
```

Somatic indices and climate were the only pair concordant after the
adjustment. Density and climate had the lowest *m*², yet this concordance
was not distinguishable from that expected between independent seasonal
series, which illustrates why a low *m*² alone is not evidence of
association.

## Lagged concordance

The hypothesized hierarchy has seven directed edges: climate to each of the
four modules, and three links between modules. Each edge is scanned from
−3 to +3 months, so a positive lag means that the first data set leads the
second. The global p-value accounts for the scan within each edge; the
edges are then adjusted within two families of hypotheses, because the four
climate edges ask whether each module responds to the same driver, whereas
the biological edges ask a different question:

```{r lagged}
climate_edges <- list(c("Climate", "Histochemistry"),
                      c("Climate", "Morphometry"),
                      c("Climate", "Density"),
                      c("Climate", "Somatic"))
module_edges <- list(c("Histochemistry", "Morphometry"),
                     c("Morphometry", "Density"),
                     c("Density", "Somatic"))
climate <- lagged_protest_pairs(dminutus_liver, pairs = climate_edges,
                                lags = 0:3, nperm = 9999, seed = 1)
modules <- lagged_protest_pairs(dminutus_liver, pairs = module_edges,
                                lags = 0:3, nperm = 9999, seed = 1)
cols <- c("x", "y", "optimal_lag", "n", "m2", "r", "p.value", "p.global",
          "p.global.adjusted")
knitr::kable(climate[, cols], digits = 3)
knitr::kable(modules[, cols], digits = 3)
```

Climate led histochemistry by three months, and this was the only edge
whose global p-value remained below 0.05 after adjustment within its
family. Notice the difference between the raw p-value at the optimal lag
and the global p-value: for climate and somatic indices, the raw p-value at
lag 0 was below 0.01, but the global p-value, which accounts for having
chosen the best of seven lags, was not significant. The contemporaneous
test above, which examines a single lag, is the appropriate one for that
pair.

The lag profile of the climate–histochemistry edge shows the minimum at
lag +3:

```{r profile, fig.alt = "Procrustes m2 against lag from -3 to 3 for climate and histochemistry; the minimum, circled and filled, is at lag 3, with global p = 0.011."}
fit <- attr(climate, "fits")[["Climate -> Histochemistry"]]
plot(fit)
knitr::kable(fit$profile, digits = 3)
```

The cyclic scheme gives a conservative check. With 12 rows and
`mirror = TRUE`, its smallest attainable p-value is 1/23 = 0.043, so a
global p-value at that bound is as strong as the scheme can show:

```{r cyclic}
cyc <- lagged_protest(dminutus_liver$Climate, dminutus_liver$Histochemistry,
                      lags = 0:3, bidirectional = TRUE,
                      permutation = "cyclic")
cyc$p.global
```

## Reading the results

The analysis supports a delayed response of liver histochemistry to
seasonal climate, of about three months, and a contemporaneous association
between climate and somatic condition. The other edges were not
distinguishable from chance with 12 monthly samples, which does not show
that they are absent: one annual cycle gives little power for weak or
delayed associations, and the optimal lag of a non-significant edge should
not be interpreted. Because the lag is estimated from a single year, it
also describes this cycle rather than a general property of the species.
